$comment: Hand-curated, unlike models.generated.json — no vendor publishes machine-readable specs, and this landscape moves slowly enough that curation is tractable. Units are the ones datasheets use: capacity in GiB (binary, as memory is sold), bandwidth in GB/s (decimal), compute in dense TFLOPS. NVIDIA and AMD headline 'AI TOPS' figures are sparse; these are halved to dense, because inference does not use structured sparsity. Every row carries a source and a status. allocatableGiB is what a model can actually have, which is below capacity on shared-memory machines. Where a platform lets the user raise that ceiling, maxAllocatableGiB is how far it can actually go, and it is never physical capacity: AMD's Variable Graphics Memory states its own maximum, and the Apple rows reserve max(8 GiB, 1/16 of RAM) for the OS.
$comment-compute: Three vendors state compute in three different units, so each row's tflops is a derivation and the derivation is the same for every row of that vendor. NVIDIA: a consumer card publishes one 'AI TOPS' headline, and it is sparse *and* quoted at the lowest precision that generation's tensor cores reach — so dense fp16 is one halving for the sparsity plus one for every precision step above it. Blackwell headlines sparse FP4, three halvings away, hence an eighth: 3352 -> 419 on a 5090, 1801 -> 225 on a 5080, 759 -> 95 on a 5060 Ti. Ada headlines sparse FP8, two halvings, hence a quarter: 1321 -> 330 on a 4090, 353 -> 88 on a 4060 Ti. Consumer Ampere has neither FP4 nor FP8 units and publishes no such headline; its dense fp16 tensor rate is 4x the FP32 shader rate (35.58 -> 142 on a 3090, 12.74 -> 51 on a 3060). The datacenter parts are transcribed rather than derived, because their datasheets state dense tensor rates directly and that shader multiple is GA10x's rather than GA100's: A100 states 312 fp16 against 19.5 FP32, which is 16x. AMD Radeon: the FP16 *matrix* rate of the AI accelerators, not the packed-vector figure published beside it — the two differ by 2x on RDNA 4. Intel: Intel publishes a peak INT8 figure and no FP16 one, and XMX runs INT8 at twice FP16 (4096 against 2048 ops per Xe-core per clock), so fp16 on the Arc rows is exactly half the stated TOPS. Apple: FP32 at 2x, from the per-GPU-core rate of that generation.
$comment-cpu-compute: The cpu-ram rows carry a *theoretical vector peak*, on the same doctrine as bandwidth: cores x base clock x two FMA pipelines x fp32 lanes x 2, with the gap between that ceiling and what a runtime achieves owned by runtimes.ts's computeEfficiency rather than pre-discounted into the row. Every row states its core count, base clock and FMA width in its note, and data/catalog.test.ts recomputes the figure from those three. Four things the formula turns on. Base clock, not boost — a boost figure is not sustainable across every core at once, and this is the conservative end of a range the efficiency constant is fitted against. Two FMA pipelines is the x86 server norm and the only per-core variable left, so a part with one would have to say so. **fp32 lanes, not fp16** — the register width is what varies, and 512 bits is 16 fp32 lanes for 64 flops per clock against 256 bits' 8 lanes for 32. AVX512-FP16 would double that again and is deliberately not counted: llama.cpp does not target the extension, and its GGUF kernels accumulate in fp32 whatever the checkpoint stores. And **Zen 4 is double-pumped**: it decodes 512-bit AVX-512 onto 256-bit datapaths in two passes, so the EPYC 9654 and Threadripper 7995WX rows compute at the 256-bit rate while stating the 512-bit width their ISA advertises. Zen 5 and Granite Rapids are full width. This basis replaced five figures that were each conservative by a different, unstated factor — catalogued over computed peak ran 0.41 to 1.12 across the five, a 2.7x spread — which meant the CPU rows could not be ranked against each other, on a surface whose whole purpose is ranking hardware. See #90.
$comment-apple-ceiling: allocatableGiB on the Apple rows is what Metal reports as its recommended working set — two thirds of RAM at 32 GiB and below, three quarters above it — because that is the figure llama.cpp warns against exceeding, and it is the default a user has before touching anything. maxAllocatableGiB is capacity minus max(8 GiB, 1/16 of RAM). Those two rules *cross over* below 32 GiB: on a 24 GiB machine the recommendation and the reserve both land on 16 GiB, and on a 16 GiB machine the reserve would put the ceiling below the default. Those rows therefore state no raiseable ceiling at all rather than one that promises less than what the machine already offers — the sysctl still exists, there is simply no figure above the default this size of machine survives.
$comment-order: Row order is display order, and nothing in the app sorts these rows: catalog.ts maps this array straight through, the Hardware picker renders DEVICES unsorted, and the Matrix renders it filtered to shipping. The sequence below is therefore curated, and these are its rules — nothing stated them until #79, which is how three rows came to break them without anything noticing. Rows are grouped by `class`, in the order the UI shows the bands: `discrete-gpu`, then `unified-soc`, then `cpu-ram`. Within a class a vendor's rows are contiguous; the order of the vendors themselves is editorial and claims nothing. Within a vendor a product line is contiguous and separated from the next by a blank line — GeForce, then RTX PRO, then the datacenter parts; Radeon then Instinct; Arc then Arc Pro; Apple's Ultra, then Max, then Pro, then Air — and inside a line the newest generation leads, with the largest or fastest bin first within a generation. Where a line is not a tiered ladder at all (the datacenter run is four generations of five unrelated products, so no ladder exists to descend) the rows run newest-released first, which is why that block reads B200, H200, L40S, H100, A100. Status is not an ordering key: a pre-release row sorts on its release date like any other, so the rumoured M5 Ultra leads the Apple run rather than sitting behind the machines it supersedes. Position then follows a fact that does not change when the machine ships, and the marker in the option label is what says the specs are not final (#69). data/catalog.test.ts enforces the first two levels, which are properties of fields every row carries. The sequence inside a product line is not machine-checked: no field encodes a line or a tier, and the only way to check it would be to add a rank to every row — which is this order restated rather than derived, and would pass by construction. The blank lines are the record of it, and they survive prettier.
$comment-note: note is reference prose for a reader who has already chosen this row: provenance, which bin the figures describe, and what the spec sheet does not say. It is not picker copy. The Hardware control shows only the short claims the app derives — pre-release status, and a raiseable allocation ceiling — and this field renders behind a disclosure below them, deliberately outside the control's accessible description, because 40 to 180 words of derivation read out on every focus is what a screen-reader user was getting instead of a choice (#68). Two rules follow from that, and both are checked over every row — the punctuation in data/catalog.test.ts, the markup in App.test.tsx — so neither is a request. Write it in whole sentences ending in terminal punctuation: this is a paragraph of its own with nothing after it to absorb a dangling clause, and a reader cannot tell prose that stops mid-clause from prose that was truncated. It used to be concatenated onto the derived claims as well, where a missing full stop read as 'raiseable to 240 GiB The allocation ceiling reserves...' on nine rows (#68) — that seam is gone, but the sentence discipline is the same discipline and lib/format.ts's sentences() still guarantees it wherever fragments are composed. And keep it prose: inline **strong**, *emphasis* and `identifiers` are rendered, and nothing else is.

devices.name: GeForce RTX 5070
devices.note: 12 GiB against the 5070 Ti's 16 at the same generation, and three quarters of its bandwidth — which is the trade this tier is actually about: the four gigabytes decide whether a 14B holds its context at all, and the bandwidth decides how fast it answers once it does.

devices.name: GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB)
devices.note: The 16 GB variant specifically. An 8 GB card ships under the same name at the same bandwidth, and a listing does not always say which — for this purpose they are different machines. Eight PCIe lanes rather than sixteen, so a spilled layer streams at 31.5 GB/s.

devices.name: GeForce RTX 4060 Ti (16 GB)
devices.note: One of the two cards that dominate the used local-LLM market, and the clearest case for reporting capacity and speed separately: it holds two thirds of what a 4090 holds at 29% of its bandwidth, so what fits and what is worth waiting for are different questions here. PCIe 4.0 x8 is 15.75 GB/s, the slowest host link in the catalog alongside the Arc B580's, so it is also among the worst cards to spill from.

devices.name: GeForce RTX 3090
devices.note: The last GeForce card with an NVLink bridge, but only two-way and only with the accessory fitted. The interconnect field records the configuration as shipped, so a bridged pair is modelled at PCIe rates here; the 40-series dropped NVLink entirely.

devices.name: GeForce RTX 3060 (12 GB)
devices.note: The other card the used market runs on, and the cheapest NVIDIA machine that holds a 12B at Q4_K_M with room for context — which is the verdict boundary this tool exists to render. Ampere has INT8 tensor cores and no FP8 ones, so an FP8 checkpoint computes here at the fp16 rate rather than at twice it.

devices.name: Radeon RX 9070 XT
devices.note: The current-generation mid-range Radeon, and the first with an FP8 matrix path. Compute here is the FP16 *matrix* rate; AMD publishes a 97.3 TFLOPS 'FP16 vector' figure beside it, which is the shader path at half the rate, and quoting that one would understate prefill by 2x on the generation that doubled matrix throughput.

devices.name: Radeon RX 7900 XTX
devices.note: 24 GiB at 960 GB/s: the standard answer to wanting a 3090's capacity without NVIDIA's pricing, and the comparison the catalog could not draw while its only Radeons were datacenter parts. RDNA 3 has no FP8 units, so an 8-bit checkpoint falls back to the fp16 rate here rather than borrowing one this card cannot dispatch. Needs ROCm or Vulkan; llama.cpp drives both.

devices.name: Radeon RX 7900 XT
devices.note: 20 GiB is an unusual capacity with no neighbour anywhere else in the catalog, which is most of the reason for the row: what the four gigabytes over a 16 GiB card buy at a given context is exactly the question the Envelope answers and a spec sheet does not.

devices.name: Instinct MI355X
devices.note: Compute was MI350X's, not this part's: the row read 2300/4600/9200 — the air-cooled sibling's dense figures — because the source pointed at the MI350 family page rather than the MI355X one. Same silicon and the same 288 GB at 8 TB/s; MI355X is the 1400W liquid-cooled bin at 2400 MHz against MI350X's 1000W at 2200, which is the ~9% this restores. Found in the pre-publish verification pass.

devices.name: Instinct MI325X
devices.note: The step that was missing between the catalogued MI300X and MI355X: the same CDNA 3 compute as the MI300X, with 256 GiB of HBM3E at 6 TB/s in place of 192 GiB at 5.3.

devices.name: Arc B580
devices.note: Intel's first row in this catalog, and $249 for 12 GiB is a price point nothing else here occupies. The fp16 figure is derived: Intel publishes peak INT8 (233 TOPS) and no FP16 rate, and XMX runs INT8 at exactly twice FP16. llama.cpp reaches it through SYCL or Vulkan. Eight PCIe lanes at 4.0, so spilling costs 15.75 GB/s.

devices.name: Arc A770 (16 GB)
devices.note: The previous Arc generation, still widely deployed and the cheapest 16 GiB in the catalog. The 8 GB card of the same name is a different machine for this purpose, which is why the capacity is in the row's name.

devices.name: Arc Pro B60 (24 GB)
devices.note: 24 GiB aimed explicitly at local inference and sold on multi-GPU boards, which is what makes it the one non-NVIDIA row worth pointing the linked-rig slider at. No msrpUsd: Intel sets no reference price and partner cards landed between roughly $500 and $800. Board power is configurable from 120W; 200W is the ceiling.

devices.name: DGX Spark (GB10)
devices.note: Fully coherent CPU/GPU pool, so no VRAM split to model. Strong prefill against modest bandwidth — the clearest case for reporting decode and TTFT separately.

devices.name: Mac Studio M5 Ultra (512 GB)
devices.note: Unreleased. Specs are press-rumour grade and must stay labelled as such in the UI — included because it is the machine people are waiting on, not because the numbers are trustworthy. The allocation ceiling reserves 32 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need — so 100% of RAM is what the sysctl parses, not what the machine survives. The GPU bin here is an assumption rather than a spec: this row is rumour-grade, and 90 TFLOPS implies a 100-core GPU at M5's per-core rate. If the part ships in more than one bin, this row is the top one, like every other Ultra in this catalog.

devices.name: Mac Studio M3 Ultra (512 GB)
devices.note: The allocation ceiling reserves 32 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need — so 100% of RAM is what the sysctl parses, not what the machine survives. This is the 80-core GPU, which 512 GiB requires — stated for the same reason as the 256 GiB row.

devices.name: Mac Studio M3 Ultra (256 GB)
devices.note: The allocation ceiling reserves 16 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need — so 100% of RAM is what the sysctl parses, not what the machine survives. This is the 80-core GPU. 256 GiB requires it, so capacity identifies the bin here — stated anyway, because capacity-implies-the-bin is the reasoning that was wrong on the three rows where it does not.

devices.name: Mac Studio M3 Ultra (96 GB)
devices.note: The allocation ceiling reserves 8 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need — so 100% of RAM is what the sysctl parses, not what the machine survives. **This row is the 80-core GPU, and it is stated because 96 GiB does not imply it — the ambiguous end of the M3 Ultra line.** Apple's base Mac Studio M3 Ultra pairs 96 GiB with a 60-core GPU and sells the larger bin as an upgrade at the same capacity, so unlike the 256 and 512 GiB rows, which require the larger part, capacity does not identify this one. At 54 TFLOPS fp16 this is the larger bin; the base machine is 60/80 of it, about 40.7, so reading this row for one overstates prefill by a third.

devices.name: Mac Studio M2 Ultra (192 GB, 76-core GPU)
devices.note: Still one of the most common large-model Macs in use, and the machine an owner has to be able to see before deciding whether to replace it — 800 GB/s against the M3 Ultra's 819 is most of the answer. The allocation ceiling reserves 12 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need — so 100% of RAM is what the sysctl parses, not what the machine survives. **The GPU bin is in the name because 192 GiB does not imply it:** M2 Ultra shipped as a 60-core and a 76-core GPU and Apple offered 192 GiB with both, so this row is the 76-core at 54 TFLOPS fp16 and a 60-core machine is 60/76 of it, about 42.7 — reading this row for one overstates prefill by 27%.

devices.name: MacBook Pro M4 Max (128 GB, 40-core GPU)
devices.note: The allocation ceiling reserves 8 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need — so 100% of RAM is what the sysctl parses, not what the machine survives. 128 GiB is only offered with the 40-core M4 Max, so capacity identifies the bin; the name states it anyway.

devices.name: Mac Studio M4 Max (36 GB, 32-core GPU)
devices.note: The Studio as it actually ships, and a different machine from the MacBook Pro row that shares the chip's name: the base M4 Max is the binned 14-core CPU / 32-core GPU part at 410 GB/s, not the 546 GB/s bin. Also the smallest machine where raising the ceiling still buys anything — Metal recommends three quarters of RAM here (27 GiB) and the 8 GiB the OS needs leaves 28. The sysctl accepts more; what loads is bounded by what the OS and the window server still need.

devices.name: MacBook Pro M1 Max (64 GB, 32-core GPU)
devices.note: The M1 generation, which had no row at all: 64 GiB at 400 GB/s is still a capable local-inference machine, and "is the new one worth it" is a question that needs both machines in the same list. The allocation ceiling reserves 8 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need. **The GPU bin is in the name because 64 GiB does not imply it.** M1 Max shipped as a 24-core and a 32-core GPU, and Apple offered 64 GiB with both, so capacity alone does not identify the part — this row is the 32-core at 21 TFLOPS fp16. A 24-core machine is 3/4 of that, about 15.7, and reading this row for one overstates prefill and understates TTFT by a third. Capacity identifies most rows in this catalog; on this one it does not, which is why the bin is stated rather than implied.

devices.name: Mac mini M4 Pro (64 GB)
devices.note: The allocation ceiling reserves 8 GiB for macOS. `iogpu.wired_limit_mb` accepts a value up to physical memory, but what actually loads is bounded by what the OS, the window server and the inference process's own unwired allocations still need — so 100% of RAM is what the sysctl parses, not what the machine survives. This is the 20-core GPU: 64 GiB is only offered with the full M4 Pro, so capacity identifies the bin, and it is stated rather than left implied.

devices.name: Mac mini M4 Pro (24 GB)
devices.note: The base M4 Pro — 24 GiB and the 16-core GPU — which is the M4 Pro most people who have one have. No raiseable ceiling is stated, and that is deliberate rather than missing: Metal recommends two thirds of RAM at this size (16 GiB) and the 8 GiB the OS needs leaves exactly the same figure, so there is nothing above the default to raise it to.

devices.name: MacBook Air M4 (16 GB, 8-core GPU)
devices.note: The Mac most Mac owners actually have, and it has a real answer rather than no answer: 10 GiB of working set at 120 GB/s takes a 4B at Q4 comfortably, a 12B slowly, and nothing above that. Metal recommends two thirds of 16 GiB, and the 8 GiB reserve the larger rows apply would put a ceiling *below* that default — so this row states none. The sysctl exists; there is no figure above the default a machine this size survives. **The compute is the 8-core GPU's, because the price is the 8-core machine's.** The $999 Air ships 8 GPU cores; 10 is a paid upgrade. M4 cores are 0.85 TFLOPS fp16 each — the M4 Pro row's 13.6 over 16 cores — so this row is 8 × 0.85 = 6.8, not the 8.5 that describes the configuration nobody gets at this price. Pairing a base price with an upgraded part overstated prefill and TTFT here by 25%, on the axis a $999 machine is least able to absorb it.

devices.name: Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (128 GB)
devices.note: Variable Graphics Memory exposes 96 of 128 GB. Bandwidth is AMD's 256 GB/s rating; measured runs near 213, and that gap is charged by bandwidthEfficiency and CLASS_BANDWIDTH_UTILIZATION rather than folded in here — see the catalog convention.

devices.name: EPYC 9755 (12-ch DDR5-6000)
devices.note: 128 cores at 2.70 GHz with two 512-bit FMA pipelines, which is 22.1 TFLOPS on the vector peak this catalog states for every cpu-ram row. Zen 5 widened the floating-point datapath to a full 512 bits, so this part does twice the work per clock per core that the two Zen 4 rows below do — which is most of the gap between them, not the extra 32 cores.

devices.name: EPYC 9654 (12-ch DDR5-4800)
devices.note: Anchors the low end of the roofline: ~6 tok/s on DeepSeek-671B Q8. CPU cores cannot saturate 12 channels of DDR5, so achieved bandwidth sits near half of nominal. 96 cores at 2.40 GHz with two 512-bit FMA pipelines, double-pumped — Zen 4 decodes a 512-bit op onto 256-bit datapaths in two passes, so the vector peak is 7.37 TFLOPS rather than the 14.7 the register width suggests. The anchor above is unaffected either way: decode on this rig is bandwidth-bound and reads no compute figure at all.

devices.name: Threadripper PRO 7995WX (8-ch DDR5-5200)
devices.note: 96 cores at 2.50 GHz with two 512-bit FMA pipelines, double-pumped as on the EPYC 9654 and for the same reason, both being Zen 4: 7.68 TFLOPS on the vector peak. Slightly above the 9654 on compute and well below it on bandwidth — eight channels against twelve — which is the trade this row exists to show, since a workstation part is the machine most readers here can actually buy.

devices.name: Xeon 6980P (12-ch MRDIMM-8800)
devices.note: Twelve channels of MRDIMM-8800 is 844.8 GB/s exactly, which is more than any EPYC row here and the reason high-bandwidth CPU inference is not an AMD-only technique. Capacity assumes one 128 GB MRDIMM per channel. 128 cores at 2.00 GHz with two 512-bit FMA pipelines, which is 16.4 TFLOPS on the vector peak. Two things it deliberately is not. Not AMX: the tile rate is roughly an order of magnitude higher, nothing catalogued here reaches it for a GGUF today, and folding it in would report a CPU's time to first token as better than a 4090's. And not the AVX512-FP16 rate of 32.8, which would be the figure if the multiply-accumulate ran in half precision — llama.cpp does not use that ISA extension, and its GGUF kernels accumulate in fp32 lanes whatever the checkpoint is stored as, so the fp32 lane count is the honest ceiling. That factor of two was the open question in #90 and it resolves against the wider figure.

devices.name: Desktop CPU (2-ch DDR5-6000)
devices.note: The floor. Included so the comparison against every other row is visible: a large model here is measured in seconds per token, not tokens per second. Modelled as 8 cores at 4.00 GHz with two 256-bit FMA pipelines, which is 1.02 TFLOPS on the vector peak. AVX2 rather than AVX-512, because that is the width a generic desktop row can promise: Intel has fused AVX-512 off its consumer parts since Alder Lake while Ryzen carries it, so assuming the wider unit would describe one vendor's machines and overstate the other's by two. Performance cores only, for the same reason — a hybrid part's efficiency cores are a count this row cannot state.
